about: Historical context for War and Peace: the real events the novel's fictional characters live through, with dates. Tolstoy gives dates in the Russian Old Style (Julian) calendar, 12 days behind the Gregorian calendar used in the West.

entries.modern: Napoleon defeated the Russian and Austrian armies at Austerlitz (in today's Czech Republic) on 2 December 1805 (20 November Old Style) — 'the battle of the three emperors'.
sources: David G. Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (1966)
entries.relationship: Real event; Prince Andrew's wounding and the sky above him are fiction set inside it.

entries.topic: The meeting of the emperors at Tilsit
match: On the thirteenth of June the French and Russian Emperors arrived in Tilsit
entries.modern: Napoleon and Alexander I met on a raft on the Niemen on 25 June 1807 (13 June Old Style); the Treaties of Tilsit (7 and 9 July 1807) made peace between France and Russia.
entries.relationship: Real event; Nicholas Rostóv's and Borís's presence there is fiction.

match: he went in a carriage to the Niemen
entries.modern: Napoleon's Grande Armée, about 450,000–600,000 men, crossed the Niemen into Russia on 24 June 1812 (12 June Old Style).
sources: Adam Zamoyski, 1812: Napoleon's Fatal March on Moscow (2004)

match: the twenty-sixth the battle of Borodinó itself
entries.modern: Borodino was fought on 7 September 1812 (26 August Old Style), about 120 km west of Moscow — one of the bloodiest single days of the Napoleonic wars, with some 70,000 casualties.
sources: Alexander Mikaberidze, The Battle of Borodino (2007)
entries.relationship: Real event. Tolstoy's own date, the twenty-sixth of August, is the same day in the Russian calendar.

match: Moscow was burned because it found itself in a position
entries.modern: Moscow burned from 14 to 18 September 1812, after the French entered it; about three quarters of the city was destroyed. Historians still debate how far the governor Rostopchin ordered it — Tolstoy's argument that a wooden city left to soldiers was bound to burn is one serious view.
sources: Alexander Mikaberidze, The Burning of Moscow (2014)
entries.relationship: Real event; Tolstoy's interpretation is still part of the historical debate.
